Q: How can I sort an array of integers? A:

The reason why the sort function behaves so weird

From the documentation:

[...] the array is sorted according to each character's Unicode code point value, according to the string conversion of each element.

If you print the Unicode point values of the array then it will get clear.

console.log("140000".charCodeAt(0));
console.log("104".charCodeAt(0));
console.log("99".charCodeAt(0));

// Note that we only look at the first index of the number "charCodeAt(0)"

This returns: "49, 49, 57".

49 (Unicode value of first number at 140000)
49 (Unicode value of first number at 104)
57 (Unicode value of first number at 99)

Now, because 140000 and 104 returned the same values (49) it cuts the first index and checks again:

console.log("40000".charCodeAt(0));
console.log("04".charCodeAt(0));

// Note that we only look at the first index of the number "charCodeAt(0)"

52 (Unicode value of first number at 40000)
40 (Unicode value of first number at 04)

If we sort this, then we will get:

40 (Unicode value of first number at 04)
52 (Unicode value of first number at 40000)

so 104 comes before 140000.

So the final result will be:

var numArray = [140000, 104, 99];
numArray = numArray.sort();
console.log(numArray)

104, 140000, 99

Conclusion:

sort() does sorting by only looking at the first index of the numbers. sort() does not care if a whole number is bigger than another, it compares the value of the Unicode of the digits, and if there are two equal Unicode values, then it checks if there is a next digit and compares it as well.

To sort correctly, you have to pass a compare function to sort() like explained here.

Q: Get current day and time in Java, to make a file name A:

tl;dr

  • Use java.time classes in Java 8+.
  • Use standard ISO 8601 formats for your generated text.

ZonedDateTime
.now( 
    ZoneId.of( "Asia/Tokyo" ) 
)
.format(
    DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern( "uuuuMMdd'T'HHmm" )  // Sorts chronologically. 
)

Modern Java

In modern Java, use the industry-leading java.time classes built into Java 8+.

To capture the current moment requires a time zone. For any given moment, the time and the date vary around the globe by time zone.

ZoneId zone = ZoneId.of( "America/Edmonton" ) ;

Or get the JVM’s current default time zone.

ZoneId zone = ZoneId.systemDefault() ;

Capture the moment.

ZonedDateTime now = ZonedDateTime.now( zone ) ;

Generate text in your specified format as defined in a DateTimeFormatter.

final DateTimeFormatter formatter = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern( "ddMMuuuuhhmm" ) ; 
String output = now.format( formatter );

ISO 8601

But your specified formatter is quite peculiar. It does not sort chronologically. And, using 12-hour clock is ambiguous, creating the same file names twice a day.

I suggest instead using the standard ISO 8601 formats. These use a T to separate date portion from time portion. And these use 24-hour clock. Their “basic” variation minimizes punctuation. For this, specify pattern "uuuuMMdd'T'HHmm".

final DateTimeFormatter formatter = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern( "uuuuMMdd'T'HHmm" ) ;

Format limitations

Keep in mind that your desired format is ambiguous in that it lacks a time zone. That may or may not work well depending on your business scenario.

Obviously, this kind of format (omitting the second and the nanosecond) only works if you are certain no more than one file per minute will be created.

Q: Efficient Cross-Correlation of 128-bit bit-strings with x86-64 CPUs A:

This is substring searching (where characters are 1 bit), so algorithms like Knuth–Morris–Pratt or Boyer-Moore could in theory be useful, but probably not worth it especially for short needles where SIMD brute-force can be good.

For long needles, brute-forcing with the first 8 bits might be a good way to obtain candidate match positions. (Or with 8-bit windows into the needle, if shifting the needle is easier than shifting the haystack. But it might not be since the needle length can be odd.) 8-bit matches with pcmpeqb / movmskb gives you a bitmask of candidate positions, which you can iterate through with tzcnt (bitpos = 8 * std::countr_zero(mask) using C++20) and blsr (mask &= mask-1; https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/blsr).
Like if(mask) { do{...}while(mask &= mask-1;) }

Brainstorming some ideas for short needles.

  • Bit-broadcast a needle to 128-bit, and XOR at every possible offset. For each offset, invert the XOR result (so XNOR) and clear lowest-set-bit of each bit-run n-1 times, where n is the needle length. (How to find if there are n consecutive set bits in a 32 bit buffer? - repeat x &= x >> 1; n-1 times and check if there are any 1 bits left. For known n, there are some more efficient sequences involving shifts by multiple bits. And Glenn Teitelbaum's more recent answer shows a recursive function which is good for compile-time-constant n.)
    Your best bet might be to just do this using SIMD on 64-bit elements, and check across the gap between elements separately. ptest can check a vector for having any 1 bits.
    Maybe we can avoid the NOT operation and invert the bithack, so we can directly find contiguous runs of zeros. But then at the end we'd have to check for there being any zeros instead of any 1s, perhaps using the CF result of ptest. But I'm not sure that's compatible with using a mask with ptest to ignore part of the input.

    The alternative using integer GPR instructions to do 128-bit shifts across the boundary involves shrd, which is ok on Intel P-cores with an immediate count such as 1: single uop although the latency is 3 cycles (from either input register to the output. Unless the same register is both inputs, then it's 1 cycle, maybe special-cased by the hardware as a rotate. But we can't take advantage of that.) On Zen 4, it's 4 uops but 2 cycle latency. (https://uops.info/ for SHRD_IMMB (R64, R64, I8)). It's terrible on Intel E-cores, like 15 uops although still only 4c latency. This would be part of a loop-carried dependency chain, but not a very long one for short needles. Runtime-variable count (in the CL register) costs 3 uops on Intel P-cores with 5c latency, 5 on AMD with still only 2 cycle latency for the data. The high half of a u128 we can just shift in zeros with a normal unsigned shift, but we'll have to ignore false-positives there.

  • Broadcast to every byte of a vector, and check against all 8 shifts of the haystack? (With an extra check across the 64-bit boundary since SIMD shifts don't cross it, unless we do extra work. Or with the AVX-512VBMI2 SIMD version of shrd (vpshrd), if we prepare a source vector to shift in from by using a byte-shift or palignr?)
    Ideally shift non-needle-matching bits into the top to avoid having to filter out false positives from there. Like shift in ~needle? No, 0101 can match 1010 when offset, if the actual end of the haystack is 1.)

  • Special-case each length and broadcast the needle until it's at least 8 bits wide, for vpbroadcastb? 2/4/8-bit needles can be fully checked that way. Like needle * 0b01010101 broadcasts a 2-bit zero-extended needle to 8-bit, or needle * 0x55555555 broadcasts to 32-bit for AVX-512 vpbroadcastd xmm, gpr. So maybe a lookup table of magic multipliers like 0101..., 001001..., 00010001.... But how do we broadcast to 128-bit if it's not a power-of-2 length? I guess right-shift the multiply result to get a high 64 bits. (Leaving up to n-1 bits zero at the top, so we'll need to ignore those when checking for matches. A true match can only start needlelen bits away from the end, so if we're using ptest to check for non-zero bits in a vector, we can use it with a mask that's -1(u128) >> n.)

This isn't a finished answer; if anyone else wants to write some actual code based on or inspired by any of these ideas, I'd love to upvote it.

I expect C++ with intrinsics like _mm_set_epi64x(hi, lo) and _mm_test_mix_ones_zeros (ptest checking the CF and ZF outputs) can get good compilers like GCC and Clang to make the asm we want, or at least fairly close. Maybe also MSVC; it tends to take intrinsics more literally which can sometimes be better for getting the asm you want from intrinsics, compared to clang's shuffle optimizer using worse instructions than what you wrote with intrinsics in tricky cases where you're being clever.

Q: How do I prevent org-mode from executing all of the babel source blocks? A:

As of Emacs 30.2 (2026) with Org 9.8, the best option that I have found is using #+property: header-args :eval never-export (or the equivalent at some other level of configuration). As others have mentioned remember to reload the buffer or C-c C-c on that line to make sure it is active. Additionally remember that you need to have :exports both or some other option that exports the results of the code block to see the result in the export.

I will also mention that the :cache yes option is also nice in similar situations, but this does not take effect at export time. :eval never-export has a similar effect, but will only 'cache' the results when the code block is interactively evaluated (i.e. outside of the export context where it changes the buffer contents by inserting the results).
